source_text: adhuc, inquit, secundum hominem dico: dum essemus paruuli, sub elementis mundi eramus positi ad deseruiendum eis. atquin non est hoc humanitus dictum, non enim exemplum est, sed ueritas. quis enim paruulus — utique sensu, quod sunt nationes — non elementis subiectus est mundi, quae pro deo suspicit? illud autem fuit, quod tum secundum hominem dixit: sed tamen testamentum hominis nemo spernit aut superordinat. exemplo enim humani testamenti permanentis diuinum tuebatur: Abrahae dictae sunt promissiones et semini eius. non dixit \'seminibus*, quasi pluribus, sed \'semini\' tamquam uni, quod est Christus. erubescat spongia Marcionis! nisi quod ex abundanti retracto quae abstulit, cum ualidius sit illum ex his reuinci, quae seruauit. cum autem euenit impleri tempus, misit deus filium suum, utique is, qui etiam ipsorum temporum deus est, quibus saeculum constat, qui signa quoque temporum ordinauit, soles et lunas et sidera et stellas, qui filii denique sui reuelationem in extremitatem temporum et disposuit et praedicauit: in nouissimis diebus erit manifestus mons domini, et: in nouissimis diebus effundam de meo spiritu in omnem carnem, secundum Iohelem. ipsius erat sustinuisse tempus impleri, cuius erat etiam finis temporis sicut initium. ceterum deus ille otiosus nec operationis nec praedicationis ullius atque ita nec temporis alicuius, quid omnino egit, quod efficeret tempus impleri et iam implendum sustineri? si nihil, satis uanum est, ut creatoris tempora sustinuerit seruiens creatori. cui autem rei misit filium suum? ut eos, qui sub lege erant, redimeret - hoc est ut efficeret tortuosa in uiam rectam et aspera in uias leues secundum Esaiam, ut uetera transirent et noua orirentur: lex noua ex Sion et sermo domini ex Hierusalem — et ut adoptionem filiorum acciperemus, utique nationes, quae filii non eramus. et ipse enim erit lux nationum et in nomine eius nationes sperabunt. itaque ut certum esset nos filios dei esse, misit spiritum suum in corda nostra clamantem: abba, pater. in nouissimis enim, inquit, diebus effundam de meo spiritu in omnem carnem. cuius gratia, nisi cuius et promissio gratiae?
pass_a_gloss: Moreover, he says: I speak according to man: while we were children, we were placed under the elements of the world to serve them. But this is not said in a human way, for it is not an example, but truth. For who, being a child - certainly in understanding, because they are nations - is not subject to the elements of the world, which they regard as God? That, however, was what he said according to man at that time: but nevertheless, no one despises or disobeys a human testament. For by the example of a human testament, he was defending the divine one: the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He did not say 'seeds', as if many, but 'seed', as if one, which is Christ. Let Marcion's sponge be ashamed! Unless, indeed, I am retracting from abundance what he took away, since it is more valid to convict him from what he preserved. When, however, the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, certainly the one who is also the God of those times, in which the age consists, who also ordained the signs of the times, sun and moon and stars, who finally disposed and predicted the revelation of his Son at the end of times: in the last days, the mountain of the Lord will be manifest, and: in the last days, I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, according to Joel. It was his to sustain the fullness of time, whose was also the end of time, just like the beginning. Meanwhile, what did that idle God do, who had no operation, no prediction, and thus no time, to bring about the fullness of time and to sustain it now that it is being fulfilled? If nothing, it is quite vain that he, serving the Creator, sustained the times of the Creator. To what purpose did he send his Son? So that he might redeem those who were under the law - that is, so that he might make the crooked straight and the rough smooth, according to Isaiah, so that the old things might pass away and new things might arise: a new law from Sion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem - and so that we might receive the adoption of sons, certainly we, the nations, who were not sons. And he himself will be the light of the nations, and the nations will hope in his name. And so, that it might be certain that we are sons of God, he sent his Spirit into our hearts, crying: Abba, Father. For in the last days, he says, I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh. To whose grace, if not to his, whose is also the promise of grace?

pass_b_english: The apostle adds that he is still speaking in human terms: while we were mere children, we were placed under the elemental spirits of the world to serve them. Yet this is no mere human illustration; it is the truth itself. For what child — certainly in understanding, since the nations are such children — is not subject to the world's elemental spirits, which they worship as gods? That statement was made 'according to man' at that time; even so, no one sets aside or adds to a human will. By appealing to the binding force of a human will, he safeguards the divine one: the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. Scripture does not say 'seeds', as if referring to many, but 'seed', as if one — and that one is Christ (Gal 3:16). Let Marcion's erasing sponge be ashamed! Unless I am simply drawing out what he deleted, since it is even more damning to convict him from the very texts he preserved.

When the fullness of time arrived, God sent his Son — the very one who is also God of those times that constitute the age, who ordained the signs of the times, sun and moon and stars, who both arranged and foretold the revelation of his Son at the end of the ages: 'In the last days the mountain of the Lord will be manifest' (Isa 2:2-3), and 'In the last days I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh,' according to Joel (Joel 2:28-29). It belonged to him to sustain the fullness of time, since the end of time was his no less than its beginning. What, then, did that idle god accomplish — a god with no operation, no prediction, and therefore no time of his own — to bring about the fullness of time and sustain it now that it is being fulfilled? If nothing, it is utterly vain that he, serving the Creator, merely sustained the Creator's times.

To what end did he send his Son? To redeem those who were under the law — that is, to make the crooked straight and the rough places smooth, according to Isaiah (Isa 40:3-4), so that the old order might pass away and the new arise: 'A new law from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem' — and so that we might receive adoption as sons, we nations who were not sons. For he himself will be the light of the nations, and the nations will hope in his name (Isa 42:6; 49:6). Therefore, to make it certain that we are God's children, he sent his Spirit into our hearts crying, 'Abba, Father' (Gal 4:6). 'For in the last days,' he says, 'I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh' (Joel 2:28-29). Whose grace is this, if not his, whose is also the promise of grace?

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal gloss, and Pass B provides a polished version with necessary scripture citations (Gal 3:16, Isa 2:2-3, Joel 2:28-29, Isa 40:3-4, Isa 42:6; 49:6, Gal 4:6) which are required for the allusions/quotes present in the Latin. All clauses, including the complex sentence regarding the 'idle God' and the 'sponge of Marcion', are preserved in meaning and agency.
